utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. I see that some Defence counsel are not present. Is it of their own choice? Shall we begin? Yes, well, let's. As was announced previously, our main issue today is the question of the documents of the Prosecution. It's a long story, as you know, which begins in January 1999, regarding a decision of the 17th of March, 1999 by the third Chamber, and it concerns the question of authenticity, one of the prime reasons behind this Status Conference. There are also documents that were sent by Mr. Krstan Simic that we shall also discuss. After that we have some other matters which we might examine, such as the question of affidavits by the Kvocka Defence; the notification by the Prosecution regarding the Kvocka expert witnesses; then also regarding the Kos Defence request for protective measures; then regarding the Radic Defence, the question of expert witnesses again and the response of the Prosecution; also, a binding order for obtaining medical documents with respect to Witnesses A and F; and with respect to the Zigic Defence, a request for lifting the confidentiality on the schedules attached to the indictment; also, a request for the signature of Mr. Ganic and another request for protective measures. But we'll go through these matters one by one. The first is the question of documents. As you know, at the end of the Prosecution case, Ms. Hollis requested that the situation regarding certain documents be clarified, that is, whether those documents had been admitted or not, and the Chamber did reply that they had been admitted. But as I have already said on another occasion, I don't think it was necessary to say that they had been admitted since they were the subject of a decision of the 17th of March, 1999. But the question of authenticity does arise. So I will give the floor to Ms. Susan Somers now who can guide us through a discussion which will lead us to a solution, I hope. Ms. Susan Somers, will you be kind enough to assist us? You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Rodrigues. Consistent with what Your Honour has just said, the plain language of the order of March 17th indicates that admission has been granted, and if I understand correctly, we're trying to find out how to interpret the language of what it means to raise a challenge to authenticity after admission. I just want to first inform the Chamber that this is a sister order to the Keraterm case in which the identical -- I guess an identical order was entered, and because there has been no challenge, everything is deemed admitted. That case, of course, will proceed in front of the other Chamber -- another Chamber. So it was not handled uniquely to this case; it was handled also for Keraterm. We have discussed it amongst ourselves, and it appears that the only way we can reconcile the status of admission upon which, of course, we have relied by virtue of the plain language and the notion of raising subsequent challenges, would be on a document-by-document basis to -- where a document, for example, would not be considered potentially self-authenticating, if an official document would normally -- if taken from an official archive and made in the course of the archivist's responsibilities or as part of the records of an institution, would not cause serious issues. Looking through the various documents that have been submitted, a goodly number of the documents, in fact, are of such a nature, including documents such as the one I think that gave rise to Mr. O'Sullivan's comment, and that was a Brdjanin document which was taken from one of the various searches in Prijedor municipality. I think any challenge that should be considered should also be considered by way of looking at what the document purports to be, and if in fact it falls in the category of an official document or pronouncement of someone like Brdjanin, I'm not even clear how Mr. O'Sullivan finds it something that he -- on behalf of his client should challenge. However, if in fact such a challenge were to be made and permitted, the best that we could offer, which I think under the circumstances, given our understanding initially, would be to have our investigators itemise locations of seizure and dates, very much in the way that Her Honour Judge Wald has requested of us, ordered us, to do where other questions where the document is not so evident arises. However, the concern is that -- is having essentially to go back for several hundred or more documents and do this when it was not necessarily contemplated that each and every document would cause or raise a challenge. In fact, the Prosecutor's case ended with no such challenge. And although the language of His Honour's order is perhaps a bit broad in that it says "during the course of the trial," it would have seemed that if the Prosecution were tendering these documents, it would have been appropriate to have raised it during the Prosecution's case. And I'm sure that is what my predecessor, Ms. Hollis, intended to clarify at the time or just prior to resting. If the Chamber for any reason is not satisfied with that, although I believe that both the language of the order and the response at the end of the Prosecutor's case - I think it was in December or December 14th, perhaps, of 2000 - when considered together and in the context of what was contemplated, I would hope that that would suffice. If there is a particular document that raises in the minds of the Chamber such an issue, then perhaps we could address it, but I don't think that there appears to be a terribly serious gap in understanding. Looking back, I read the two orders, the two events together, both the issuance of the decision and Ms. Hollis's timely approach to the Chamber, and the Chamber's having effectively, I would say, waited for a response from the Defence which was not forthcoming. And that should be determinative of the issue. If the Chamber asks of us something else, of course we will do what we have to do, but I don't think -- from just looking at things, it seems to have been covered. If the Chamber would indulge me one more comment, I'm sorry. Because of reliance on what appears to have been an issue put to rest, it would work a tremendous hardship and disadvantage to the Prosecution to have to revisit each and every document if, in fact, that were what the Defence were trying to assert. And I would ask the Chamber at this time also to consider that the fairness issues that go into reliance on decisions of the Chamber and on the content of proceedings. So I wanted to make sure that I indicated for us it would be a tremendous, tremendous and unexpected burden where we had no reason to believe we were in a different position other than the way we finished out the year when the Prosecution rested. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think my first impression, if I may convey it, is that I think we're all at fault, and I'm speaking of this Chamber, because as you know, I have a lot of respect for the work of others, but we are to resolve this issue. The Prosecutor, because it accepted this from the beginning, Ms. Hollis did not explicitly raise this question of authenticity. She just asked whether the documents had been admitted or not. Why, if they had already been admitted? The Chamber, because we ourselves did not take into consideration this question which was, in a sense, concealed, if I might put it that way, because eventually we decided, as Ms. Susan Somers said, in our decision of the 14th of December, we ruled that the documents were admitted, but we did not address this matter which could be an obstacle. And the Defence has the merit of drawing our attention to the fact that there is a problem, and I think that there is a problem and that is what we have to deal with now. I will give the floor to the Defence in a moment. I think that the axis of the discussion could be the question of the ruling of the 17th of March, the question of challenging the authenticity of documents during the trial. You see, does that mean during the Prosecution case until the Prosecution rested its case or at the end of the whole trial? You see, this is rather confusing, because how can the Prosecutor complete its case if the documents it relied on could, at any moment, be challenged until the end of the trial? Therefore, what does this mean, that the Defence can challenge the authenticity of documents which are admitted? As I have already said, this may be a personal opinion, but I think that before admitting a document, the authenticity of that document should be discussed; otherwise, it is a futile endeavour. Another axis of discussion could be: What does this mean, that the Prosecutor should address the questions relating to the authenticity of documents admitted during the rebuttal? So these things are a bit complicated for our present situation. Therefore, this Chamber would suggest that we have this discussion, and then at the end I think the solution is simple: If the Defence wishes to challenge the authenticity of documents, it should say so now, providing the reasons and how they intend to do it. If not, I think we should overcome all these matters by saying either the documents are admitted unconditionally, all of them; or if the Defence needs to investigate the situation, to reflect upon the situation and the significance of such a decision, the Chamber may give some time to the parties to review the matter and come back to the Chamber, upon which the Chamber can rule. I have given some highlights for the discussion. I hope you will forgive me for my own personal perceptions of this discussion. I will give the floor now to Defence counsel, therefore, Mr. Krstan Simic, first.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for some time now, I have a feeling that there is confusion here and I am not able to find my way around when it comes to exhibits. Let me give you an example. In the cross-examination of Mr. Kvocka, my learned friend offered certain documents, and I have them listed here, number 3/186, 3/201, 3/203. We, again, had our own documents, D41/1, and so on and so forth. All the time I was confident that the submission made by the Prosecution in the brief made by the Prosecution, and in my own brief, there was a list of the documents which the Defence intends to use if need be. Everything functioned well until, during the cross-examination, the Prosecution presented a document, had it marked for identification, we objected or did not object to it, and then the Chamber ruled on the admission or non-admission of each document. That is a record of the documents that we have. As a result of all this, there has been some confusion with the numbers, and we are still having some confusion with numbers. As far as this Defence team is concerned, we do not challenge the authenticity of those documents which, during the case, were presented to witnesses, either the witnesses of the Prosecution or the Defence, and when the Defence was able to say whether it objects or not to the admission of such documents. Those documents that were admitted, even if we objected to them and the Chamber admitted them, we can't retroactively challenge that decision. However, we cannot accept that whole list that arrived in the form of a tender as to what will be used because we were not aware that they would be used during the examination. As I'm on my feet, I'd like to raise another matter linked to documents. Ms. Somers here, on a number of occasions, mentioned that these documents had been confiscated, that they were under lock and key of the Prosecution. The Defence has absolutely no access to those documents. We spent an hour talking here about whether Mr. Kvocka signed or did not sign a solemn declaration. The man does not remember, which is quite normal. He may have signed one. And then today, we are shown a solemn declaration, whose authenticity is challenged, it was produced today, so we wonder whether such a statement may exist for Mr. Kvocka too. We simply have no access to documents except those which the Prosecutor is kind enough to show us. So this is a very serious problem for us. Maybe they have a document where it says that somebody was the commander, that somebody was the warden, and I think that is why Mr. Fila requested that he have access to those documents. This is a question that needs to be resolved by the Defence being given access to those documents. The statement we are getting is, "We seized this, it is ours, and we have no ability to review them," and I consider this to be a very serious shortcoming. As for the documents that we did not object to their admission and which were admitted by the Chamber, we are not challenging their authenticity; but the documents that were not discussed, I think needs to be reviewed. We have to know which document we are talking about, whether it is authentic or not, whether we can admit it or whether we can object to it. Of course, the final decision is with Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There seems to be a minor methodological point here. No, please remain seated, Mr. Krstan Simic. Ms. Susan Somers, do you wish to respond to each counsel or all of them together? Could you wish to respond to what Mr. Simic has said, or shall I give the floor to the other counsel and then you can respond to all of them? It's up to you to choose.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Simic has raised an issue that is unrelated to the bigger issue which the Chamber has raised, and that is 66 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, excuse me. Is your reply that you prefer to respond to each individual Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to know. My preference would be, of course, to rule out any discussion of 66(B) because that is not the discussion before the Chamber right now, and that's what Mr. Simic just raised. We're talking now about the order of the previous Chamber that was seized with this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Go ahead, then, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What Mr. Simic is referring to is a request that would have to be made. There's no other basis for making it other than pursuant to Rule 66(B), which request has been made by Mr. Fila and is in the process of being completed by Mr. Jovan Simic. That is the only request, other than Rule 68, wherein documents are the subject of obligatory turnover by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I don't understand that, Ms. Somers. I know what 66 and 66 reciprocal, but if the Prosecution gives a long list of documents which it wishes to have admitted as -- do you mean to say you don't have to show the Defence the documents which you want to have the Court admit?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Those are not the same documents. Mr. Simic is referring to what is called the Prijedor collection, which are not necessarily in the binders that were the subject of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, just indulge me for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You're not suggesting that if the Prosecution has as whole list of exhibits or documents that it wishes to have admitted, that the Defence doesn't have a right at some point to look at them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It would depend on when we're trying to put them in, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: How can you argue that they should just be admitted and then, and then say but the Defence can't, can't look at them at any point.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think the ones that were the subject of admission were available to the Defence to look at. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Correct, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What Mr. Simic is talking about is this collection of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There were documents which may or may not ever come before this Chamber, depending on the need to respond, perhaps, to a point on cross or if it's raised during the Defence's case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And they're not in the binders of exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, they're not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: No, it's not your fault. It's useful to get those two categories established.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There are a number of other documents which were seized from a number of locations, and that -- which is why, Your Honour Judge Rodrigues, I just wanted to segregate that. I think the issue of the three binders from the March 17th order is quite separate. Mr. Simic at no time ever presented a request pursuant to 66(B). Had he done, so we would have examined it, as we're examining now the request by the other counsel. Otherwise, I think it might be best if we responded to all the comments of Defence counsel on the other matters, and of course, we'll always come back to the authenticity being a matter of weight if in fact -- okay, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. O'Sullivan, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. My position on this matter relates to a distinction which may exist between admissibility and authenticity, and I say it may exist because Rule 89 governs this matter, I submit. And the reason why there may be a distinction between admissibility and authenticity is because if we look at Rule 89(C), that rule states that the Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value. But if we continue down in that rule to subrule (E) it says, "A Chamber may request verification of the authenticity of evidence obtained out of court." In my submission, the previous Chamber, Trial Chamber III with Judge May presiding, admitted the documents submitted in January 1999 on the basis of Rule 89(C) and did not require at that time any proof of authenticity. Indeed, on the 11th of January, 1999, in the Prosecutor's request for admission, the Prosecution stated that the issues relating to authenticity and reliability should not preclude their admission at this stage. The Prosecution relied entirely on Rule 89(C). And arguably, and I think clearly, a year before this trial began, approximately, these documents were submitted to the parties and the Chamber for admission on the basis of their being relevant. There was never a hearing, any evidence adduced, as to issues of authenticity. Now, that application of Rule 89 is the widespread practice of this Tribunal, in my submission, where starting with, as my learned friend Mr. Saxon said earlier today, that the Tadic case and, more importantly, the Celebici judgement, the Chamber in Celebici ruled that under 89(C) relevant documents may be admitted, but the issue of authenticity will go to weight accorded to those documents, if any, at the close of proceedings in final argument. Now, I'll just briefly, very briefly, Your Honour, quote from Celebici. The Chamber said this: "The Trial Chamber wishes to make clear that the mere admission of a document into evidence does not in and of itself signify that the statements contained therein will necessarily be deemed to be an accurate portrayal of the facts. Factors such as authenticity and proof of authorship will naturally assume the greatest importance in the Trial Chamber's assessment of the weight to be attached to individual pieces of evidence." It seems to me that in this case, our trial, in January 1999, we proceeded on the basis of Rule 89(C), the documents being admitted as being relevant and having probative value on their face, but there was no evidence led at that time in regards to authenticity. And when this whole matter arose a short time ago, perhaps two weeks ago, the objection was based on the fact of the formulation that my learned friend used in cross-examining a witness by stating that you have a document signed by a certain individual, and the objection was that there was no proof in the record to support that assertion by the Prosecution, and Your Honours' upheld the objection precisely because there was no proof of authenticity. So the rules allow two cases to go, in my submission. 89(C) can be read in conjunction with 89(E), and authenticity can be made a condition precedent to admission. On the other hand, as has happened in this case and others, documents may be admitted under 89(C) alone, and the issue of weight or authenticity is tied to weight ultimately when all the evidence is heard. And my objection is based on the latter, the procedure having been followed here, that the burden lies with the Prosecution to prove every element of its case, that is our position, including proof, ultimately, of the authenticity of its documents and the weight that Your Honours can accord to those documents, if any. So that is my position, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Let me just ask you this: Does that mean Ms. Somers' great concern about all the documents which have been used up to now, does that mean, in your view, that if the Defence has not, heretofore, raised a particular concern about authenticity and/or proof of authorship, et cetera, that those documents can remain, subject to some argument you might make in the closing statement or something about weight, but they can remain admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I thought. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. O'Sullivan, I also have a question for you. I was listening to the French interpretation which was late; I was on the same channel and now it's free. You have heard me, Mr. O'Sullivan, when I spoke about Rule 65 ter (E). Were these documents submitted or tendered into evidence within the framework of Rule 65 ter, that is, during the pre-trial procedure? I no longer remember if, at that period of time, we still had this Rule 65 ter. Supposing that it was already there, how do you read the provision that the Prosecutor has to submit a list of exhibits and also to indicate whether the Defence objects to its authenticity or not; that is to say, did the Defence, at that time, already have a standpoint about that, have a viewpoint about this issue? I agree with you and your interpretation of Rule 89(C). We understand what you mean, in view of the legal system you come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, in response to your question, Your Honour, in the pre-trial phase in these proceedings, we were operating under Rule 73 bis, which is identical in wording to 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- so I'll refer to 65 ter. If we look at 65 ter (E)(v), that's the basis upon which an order was made by Judge May for the Prosecution to submit its documents. I think we can look at the plain language used by the Prosecution in its submission of 11 January 1999, the one to which I referred before, there is no agreement as to stipulation by the Defence; 65 ter saying, "... the list of exhibits the Prosecutor intends to offer, stating where possible whether the Defence has any objection as to authenticity." Well, the Prosecution motion is silent in that regard because it appears there was no previous stipulation by the Prosecution, and therefore the Prosecution relied on Rule 89(C). Of course, the parties can always stipulate to authenticity, but in this case, I submit there was no inclusion in the Prosecution's filing of January 1999 because there had been no agreement between the parties as to authenticity, and therefore they were not admitted with that condition having been established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From your point of view, Mr. O'Sullivan, is there a problem? And if yes, do you have a solution or a suggestion to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: My response, quite simply, is that it's a matter for each party to present its case as it sees fit and to prove its case as it sees fit. That's as far as I can take that point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much, Mr. O'Sullivan. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the legal system I come from provides for the submission of original documents to the court within a certain period of time. It is, of course, possible to use photocopies for the purposes of the trial for a limited period of time. However, since we are sure that the OTP did not receive copies, photocopies of the documents, but that it made its photocopies later on on the basis of original documents, that initial, original document which is in the possession of the OTP must simply be submitted to the Registry. And then after that, if I think, or any of my colleagues from the Defence - the same goes for the Prosecution if I am the one tendering the document - if a challenge is made in respect of that document, then we have to prove that the document in question is not an original. Second, if we should accept that, in view of the circumstances, those documents were obtained in a somewhat unusual fashion, by use of weapons, tanks, and others which is not a customary procedure to follow, then in that case, it is necessary for the party which obtained the documents in such an unusual fashion to provide us with the list of documents which were obtained, where and when they were obtained, and then there should be a cross-examination conducted before this Chamber with a view to confirming that that, indeed, was the case. I do respect the opinion of my colleague, Ms. Somers, that if we go back to all of these documents, it would then lead us to the end of this trial ad callendas graechas, and the only practical solution which I can suggest would be the following: Let us see what remains in dispute between us. Then once we identify points of dispute, in those cases, we should be shown the original of the document and then we should also be told about the circumstances of how the document was obtained, by whom, and where, and I think that would be enough, and that individual should come to testify. Let me remind you that within the past two years of this trial, we were faced with this problem only during the cross-examination of Mr. Kvocka, it was only at that moment that this problem arose, and only two, three, maybe ten documents are in dispute. That is the way I see this problem. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Fila. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. We should like to take your suggestion and think a little about this very complex matter, and we will guide ourselves with the principle of equality of parties. However, at this point, I should like to join in with my colleagues, Mr. Krstan Simic, Jovan Simic, and Mr. Fila, which relates to the issue of access to documents. We are still searching for a number of documents in respect of which we are sure that they exist, or that they existed at one point in time. I will just give you a few examples. In Omarska, many individuals, many victims gave prior written statements to the investigators of the OTP. Later on, in case of some other victims - and I can tell you exactly which victim I have in mind; he testified under a pseudonym - it was stated that the statement was adequately interpreted and that the witness was given an opportunity to correct his statement if necessary. So those statements can be, indeed, used in some cases. Same goes for Keraterm. It is very strange that, in case of a massacre which happened on the 24th of July, 1993, not a single document was submitted by the OTP. I have to say that at this point, the Defence does not have any such documents either. However, from the information that we have heard, we are sure that there are a number of official documents relating to this particular incident, or that there were such documents at one point in time. Therefore, we should like to be given access to the documents seized, or at least access to the list of such documents, and I'm sure that we will be able to find something that we -- some of the things that we've been looking for. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Masic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in accordance with Rule 66(B) we contacted the Prosecutor with a letter, and we hope that the Prosecutor will give us an opportunity to have access to the documents which are of interest for us before the beginning of our case. As regards the authenticity of document, I accept everything that has been stated in respect of that issue by my colleague Mr. O'Sullivan. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have heard several Defence counsel on this issue, and I hope that you can respond, Ms. Somers. However, before you do that, I should like to address the issue which was raised by Mr. Fila, that is, that the originals should be submitted to the Registry. I think that I spoke about the issue this morning that regards amendment of Rules of Procedure and Evidence, in particular, Rule 41. There is a new wording of this particular rule which says that material evidence collected during the investigation -- I don't quite remember the wording, but you have the rule in front of you. In accordance with that rule, the originals which are in the possession of the Prosecutor must be submitted at the end of the case. In that case, the public in general can have access to the originals of those documents. So this is the amendment of Rule 41. I hope you all have it, and you can draw appropriate conclusions from the new wording of the rule. We are not going to debate the matter ad callendas graechas. I hope you know what it means. It's something that does not actually exist. So I think we have to be able to finish before that time elapses. Ms. Somers, for your response, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Once again, Your Honour, there were a number of issues just raised before the Chamber, many of which have nothing to do with the question which the three Honourable Judges are trying to have some ideas on resolution for. If going back to the original issue, which is what import in reading is given to the order of Judge May's Chamber, if in fact -- and again, it does not cite to the provisions upon which it was based on -- on which His Honour Judge May had based his order. However, 89(C) says, "The Chamber may admit relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value"; but (E) says, "a Chamber may request verification of the authenticity of evidence obtained out of court." Judge May's order appears to transfer the matter to the Defence. The Defence are at liberty -- I read from the order: "The Defence are at liberty to challenge the authenticity of any of the documents during the trial, and the Prosecution shall deal with any issues raised as to the authenticity of the documents so admitted by way of rebuttal." If in fact admission has been made and there are questions raised during -- either during proceedings or during argument, it would seem that weight, the issue of weight would be the crucial issue upon which the Chamber would focus its attention, having decided there was relevance which would have been the threshold finding for admission. And we think that would be perhaps the best resolution of the immediate issue, given some of the ambiguities which unfortunately have arisen, maybe because at the time of issuance of the order there were no questions raised and that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. two years have gone by with no additional questions raised, effectively. It would seem that that would square with the rules and with what appears to have been -- and again, having not been present, it is a bit difficult for me to look past anything that I see in writing, but what appears to have been, and it seems may -- this may also be borne out by Mr. O'Sullivan's reading of it, the intention of the Chamber. And so it would seem a resolution consistent with what appears to have been the intent to treat as admitted, and should particular questions arise, to so note, and those questions should be raised in argument so that the Chamber is reminded at the time that there was an issue raised. I think under all circumstances, that would be the most equitable and consistent with what appears to have been the understanding of both sides. Again, I wish I could cast some light on what took place, but it is nowhere indicated. And just by virtue of a lapse of time, the noticeable lack of objection by the Defence in the course of two years, and the other events which have allowed the Prosecution to rest its case without any type of concern as to the security of admission or not, this may be the best for all parties. As we would do with any documents, for example, which the Defence may choose to put in. If we have a question, if our objections go to an issue of authenticity, we will, of course, so note. And if admitted over objection, we shall remind the Chamber in our arguments of these issues, and I think that's incumbent on the parties to do. But I think that it would seem that that may, if the Chamber feels this covers all aspects of possible concern, be a reasonable resolution. The other issues which were raised by various learned friends opposite concerning searches and what may or may not be in the possession of the Prosecution, except under Rule 68, and the searches under 68 have been effected. Those matters lay in the hands of the Judges who issued lawful search warrants, and there is -- my understanding is there is no standing on the part of persons from whose custody, actual or constructive, these items were not [sic] seized, and that would include any and all of the accused. Therefore, any request to see documents which are not used by the Prosecution specifically would have to fall within the materiality section, material to the Defence. There are several prongs to 66(B), and this is the basis for the application or for the request made by my two learned friends opposite. That determination is being made in accordance with the jurisprudence of the Tribunal, so that is a separate issue. I don't know if there is a third issue that I should address, but I think those would be the overriding concerns. And if the Chamber might consider letting us know if there's some other avenue it sees, we would be very grateful, because really looking at it from a very common sense point of view, it would seem that the ability to argue at the end issues of potential objections to authenticity or questions would be a particularly useful resolution. I must bring to the Chamber's attention, having looked at the, cursorily looked at the terms of the new rule that has just been brought in, there will, of course, be issues where there are sister cases -- for example, this case is a sister case to Keraterm, which is a sister case to the ARK investigations and trials, which may also have shared evidence with Krajisnik and Plavsic. So I don't know at what point the Registry will find a mechanism by which, if a document in the original is given to the Registry for, let's say, the Omarska case, how it will find some means by which that very same document can also be used for the sister cases which have the same operative facts or similar ones. And I just wanted to bring this to the Chamber's attention because I'm confident that all members of the Chamber are aware of how cases either come in piecemeal here and are tried because of serial surrender or because of other similar factors, perhaps severance. But this will always be an issue, and I'm hopeful that there will be some means of address to this by the Registry as well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Somers. I think that we have just heard a suggestion by Ms. Somers here. I don't know whether the Defence wishes to reply to this very practical suggestion which was made by Ms. Somers. Mr. Simic? No. Mr. O'Sullivan?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have a question on your practical suggestion. Are you suggesting that it all be taken care of in argument? For instance, the other day we had a sort of unsigned un-source-indicated unsource list of people theoretically in category 1 at Omarska, okay? We didn't -- it wasn't signed by anybody. We don't know where it came -- you told us it was seized. You would say that then if Mr. O'Sullivan, I'm just using an example, got up and objected to that document being used, that it should just be handled when closing argument came, you would argue, or are you still going to abide by your earlier offer that at least you would, you would share with us by affidavit or somewhere else a few details of when and where it was seized; and in the case of some documents which are challenged because we only have a Xerox copy and can't see the signature, whether the signature comes in. I just wasn't clear whether you were -- what you just talked about weight and argument, you think it should all be handled just two people arguing. Because as a fact finder, I don't find that satisfactory. If you tell me it was seized and the other side says, "We don't have enough, enough proof," and I don't find argument to be a satisfactory way to solve something. I would find it a satisfactory way if there were something which reasonably authenticated it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Which is what I had in my hands. I had not gotten to point B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Of course in instances, and there were specific instances where a document -- it is not evident, perhaps, even from the face of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: About -- for example, if it were found in archive, that should be indicated, and absolutely, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay, all right, all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It's only fair, it's only appropriate. I will deal, of course, at the end of this, because I believe one of the items on today's agenda was the moving into evidence of the Kvocka cross-examination documents, and this was indeed one of those matters, so I will address specifically that document as well as the other matter that Your Honour Judge Wald raised. But yes, of course, we're preparing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right, all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: If I can respond briefly to that question raised by Judge Wald. It may, in fact, arise in this or any other trial that a party has a document admitted and, for one reason or another, cannot satisfy the fact-finder as to authenticity, in which case argument will follow and the fact-finder must decide what weight to attribute to that document. So there are issues that go beyond provenance of documents which are relevant to authenticity. For certain documents, that may be all you need; in certain cases, it may not be enough. Ultimately, if a party does not or cannot prove its documents to the satisfaction of the Chamber, that is argued by the parties at the end of the case, whether it's a Prosecution document or a Defence document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now that we have discussed the matter, the Chamber will decide. Another question we have here, if I may call it the practical side of all this, are the documents which the Kvocka Defence, that is, Mr. Krstan Simic, has sent to us. As we have said, there were some documents which were already admitted into evidence by -- tendered by the Prosecutor. I think that the Registry has separated and identified those documents and I think now Mr. Krstan Simic has received their report. After that, we have to see whether you are satisfied with the result of that effort, that is, whether you are asking now only for the admission of those documents, and, on the other hand, to see what is the position of the Prosecution. So, Mr. Krstan Simic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have received a document in which the differences have been stated which are the result of the method of work applied. So the following documents remain in dispute, documents tendered by the Defence: D41/1, the request for an investigation by the military prosecutor of the 7th of August, 1995, and a decision on the investigation of the military tribunal, and a decision that Andza Jovic did not give her vehicle for use. Also, a large number of documents have been admitted from our list; however, the discharge papers from Miroslav Nisic, discharge from hospital, who was injured in a shooting on the 30th of May, 1992, that document has not been admitted. Also, a document tendered by us, it is an abstract from the penalties for Miro Behanovic [sic] from the 12th of August, 1994 -- I apologise, the name is Emir Beganovic - Emir Beganovic - rather than Miro Behanovic. Emir Beganovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, does that document have a number? Has it been marked for identification? I'm sorry for interrupting you. You mentioned the document D41/1, and in that same category, I have the document D45/1. Those two documents were tendered but have still not been admitted. I don't know if you are talking about both at the same time or whether you are talking about two different documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise, I wasn't focused enough. Some documents were given numbers by us, for instance, D44/1, and we established that it has been marked 2/3-70 by the Prosecution. If we were to continue using our own numbers, then the hospital discharge papers for Miroslav Nisic would be numbered 48/1. Then the records on penalties for Emir Beganovic should be marked 49/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, I'm really afraid we are going to get lost altogether. You're talking about 49/1, but in the list of the Prosecution documents I have from the Registry, the highest number is D47/1. Has the Registry given you this list? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and I am going on from that last number, giving you new numbers so as to avoid all confusion, carrying on from that last number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but you've gone on to 48 and 49. What do you wish to tell us? I'm sorry. I'm lost; maybe others too. Maybe it's my fault. Surely, it's my fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I received a document from the Registry in which documents were marked which were not the subject of discussion or adoption. According to that document, they have not yet been marked for identification, and I have in front of me five such -- rather, six such documents. My intention now was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're talking about documents, Mr. Simic, which were admitted by the Prosecutor or, rather, were tendered by the Prosecution and also by the Defence; is that what you mean? Because there are documents, as you know, that have already been given numbers by the Prosecution, and they have different numbers given by the Defence. According to what I have, there are seven such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, but, Your Honours, there are some documents which are different, and I'm talking about the differences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're talking about documents -- you're talking about seven documents on which a decision needs to be taken, a decision on their admission; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, documents which were not marked either by the Prosecution or the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And there are seven documents again of that kind?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Six documents. But there are five sentences of the military tribunal which could be all under one number. May I list those documents and give them a number, going on from the last number that we had?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those documents were never tendered by the Prosecution, so it is the Defence that has requested that they be admitted; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Susan Somers, you were going to say that you have no objections; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I wish I could be that charitable, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would facilitate things.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'll let the Court know that we have prepared a written response for those documents. If the Chamber recalls, our objection on the military court was simply that it cited a provision of law without submitting the actual law, and we were waiting for Mr. Simic to present the law upon which these convictions were based, and that would have alleviated it, and that's all we had been waiting for. We had some relevance issues, but we'd be happy to see what the law says that formed the basis for those judgements, the actual violation under which these individuals were charged, and that would help us enormously. So if that were provided, that could, perhaps, knock out or eliminate some of these problems. We have drafted, ready for filing, a document which itemise our responses to those few controversial items. Would that be helpful, to have that in front of all parties? Otherwise, there is a lot of guessing and making up numbers. Would that be something I could submit to counsel and to the Chamber, and then perhaps at the end of some session, the Chamber would -- okay, great.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, you see, Mr. Simic, I think that Ms. Susan Somers really does want to facilitate our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, but I would ask, since the cross-examination of Mr. Kvocka is over, I would ask to be allowed to present those documents, and I will respond to Ms. Somers once we receive her responses. Allow me to read them out so that they be part of the record, and then we can comment on them, if necessary, at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you are asking is to identify those documents now; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and for them to go down in the record as my suggestion for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead, please. Go ahead, please, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. So D48/1, hospital discharge papers for Miroslav Nisic, who was injured on the 30th of May, 1992 and was discharged from hospital on the 18th of June, 1992; 49/1, an abstract from the record of convictions for Emir Beganovic; 50/1, an information, dated the 13th of July, 1992, on the implementation of the conclusions of the Crisis Staff of Prijedor municipality. Also, judgements of the military tribunal, dated the 16th of June, 1995, against Vladislav Vekic; and of the same tribunal, dated the 20th of April, 1995, again Zeljko Kvetma; again, of the same tribunal, the 20th of April, 1995 against Dzuro Petkovic; of the same tribunal, dated the 24th of July, 1995, against Svetko Masic; and a judgement of the military tribunal, dated the 27th of February, 1995, against Zoran Karenovic; all those judgements would be marked as D50 -- sorry, D51/1, and they could be marked A, B, and C as they are all part of one and the same judgement and they illustrate the possibilities of abandoning police or military units. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Document 52/1, D52/1, is the case history of Emir Zjakic, son of Ahmet, of the 11th of June, 1992, also injured in a shooting of the 30th of June; D53/1 is an announcement of the Ministry of Justice of Republika Srpska, dated the 14th of December, 2000, that it never issued any document on the appointment of Miroslav Kvocka as an official serving as the warden of the prison in Omarska. Your Honours, those are documents that are in addition to documents tendered by the Defence and by the Prosecution, and that would complete the list of documents being tendered by the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think things are a little clearer now. These documents that have now been identified and whose admission will be discussed, Ms. Somers will respond as soon as she has the abstract from the mentioned law. On the other hand, if I remember correctly, Ms. Susan Somers mentioned some documents that you would like to tendered on behalf of witness Markovski, I think, and within the framework of the cross-examination of Mr. Kvocka at a minimum. So we would now like to address that matter. Do you remember? Do you recollect? If you're not ready for it, we can find another opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No, thank you very much for the opportunity. On the Kvocka cross, that, of course, I would like to deal with while it's fresh in everybody's minds. I can't recall anything outstanding on Markovski. There may be another witness. I think the Chamber did admit the next day after Mrs. Kvocka's testimony, it was the day Your Honour Judge Wald was not feeling well and the next day the Chamber dealt with two exhibits. Perhaps that may have been -- because I recall Your Honour Judge Rodrigues mentioning something, and that was the next day. I think that was 201 and 202. Those were dealt with by the Chamber and admitted. And then specifically there are several from the examination of Mr. Kvocka that I would like to make sure I move into evidence. Would now be a convenient time to do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you have the necessary element; if not, we can grant you some other time and another opportunity. But I would like to remind you, yes, I remember the moment when Judge Wald had to leave and she wasn't feeling too well, and you were just about to ask for admission. And there was another when I said we can deal with it at a Status Conference. I think that was at the end of the cross-examination of Mr. Kvocka. You asked me whether you could do that at a Status Conference, and I said "Yes, of course." Do you remember that? I don't have my notes on me just now, but on another occasion I could maybe prepare myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: My concern was that, effectively that the cross-examination of Mr. Kvocka be considered open until I had an opportunity to move these documents in. Your Honour correctly recalled. And if I may run through them now, I have the numbers. It really should be a quick exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: First document was Prosecution Exhibit 3/185 which was tendered, and it is the order regarding firearms training involving Mr. Kvocka purporting to be signed by Hasan Talundzic. That was the first one. Mr. Kvocka was asked about this and, in fact, commented on the nature of the firearms training. That would be the first. Second is 3/186 which was of 18 May 1991. It was signed -- purported to be signed by Fikret Kadiric, the then commander from Prijedor. The Chamber rightly reminded us that there was a problem in the translation which was remedied that day, so the English translation is correct, and I would move also -- that was put to Mr. Kvocka as well. The English translation, I think, was given a revised number of 3/186 bis. The next document was also one that caused a problem of my learned friends opposite on 3/188, which was a statement under oath that had for some reason a parenthetical addition of "loyalty oath." We checked with the translation section and they indeed have reviewed their own translation and have submitted a corrected, revised edition which we have for Chamber and counsel. And indeed, there is no mention of "loyalty," so the solemn oath is the correct -- it's called "Solemn Declaration." If I may offer this, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, this exhibit will be marked 3/188 bis, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This is the notation that I have. This I believe came from discussion in the courtroom. Is that correct, how it was marked? Yes, Your Honour. I'm sorry, no, I'm sorry. I beg your pardon. The solemn declaration, no, no, that's 3/188. The solemn declaration that you have in your hands, Your Honour and counsel, 3/188. There was no new number assigned or discussed. The 186 bis was the revised translation of the work schedule of 18 May. What I have just distributed to the Chamber is 3/188. There was no changes, simply a correction of the translation. If the Chamber should issue a bis number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Why are you distributing this to us?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This is a correction of a translation. What the Chamber had been given while we cross-examined the accused was a document which had, for no explanation, "loyalty oath" in parentheses. It was wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But the Registry doesn't replace documents, so if there is a document already and this is being brought to replace it, it has to have -- be marked bis. But Madam Registrar is here. What is your position? This is a document replacing the other one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes. This is what the Chamber had asked us for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I think we need to know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us hear, you Madam Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the record there is a document 3/188. It is an English version, and there is another one which is the B/C/S version. And now we are given a corrected version of 3/188, so it will have to be marked as 3/188 bis, and we have no objection on the understanding that the only valid document will be 3/188 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Madam Registrar, what is the number of the document we have just received?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3/188 bis, the revised English version of the document 3/188.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Somebody should pay me for my effort. I'm sorry, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The next document was 3/189 which was a list of the hours worked by various police employees in June of 1992 with Mr. Kvocka appearing on a particular page. We did inquire of the accused about this document, and we ask to have that moved in, please. Then moving on, if the Chamber is ready, in the course of asking a question about a document that purported to have been from a statement taken of a Serb individual in Bosnia in army custody, was 3/199, I have, perhaps after the fact, studied the rulings of that Chamber, and I would not be permitted under this Chamber's rulings to even attempt to put in a statement, another person's statement under these circumstances. So any attempt to have moved it in would be withdrawn by me, and I simply referred to the document as a -- for purposes of credibility. And in fact, the question had been asked of me to check signature. I was unable -- on the typed version, unable to confirm any signature. However, there does exist a version in the handwriting allegedly of the individual which does bear a signature. However, I think it becomes moot because I'm only using it for purposes of credibility, so that would be withdrawn for any other purposes. As I indicated, the Chamber had previously admitted 3/201 and 3/202 which respectively are the Slobodna Bosna interviews of what we've referred to euphemistically as the Bennett interview, and then also contained in the Radio Prijedor, Free Radio Prijedor, sorry, that was previously admitted under Mrs. Kvocka's testimony. Then 3/203 is the 24 June 1998 interview between investigator Bob Reid and Miroslav Kvocka. We would, of course, move that -- seek to move that into evidence. 3/204 was the list of category 1 persons from the Omarska Collection Centre about which all members of the Bench had a question, and we have -- I'm not sure of the best way logistically to show this to the Chamber. One of the issues raised by one of my learned friends opposite was the appearance in English of writing "Omarska category 1." I'm happy to report, very happy to report that it was a PostIt on the original, and that when scanned, unfortunately, the PostIt was scanned along with the document. However, the original, in fact, does exist, and I can provide -- if I can circulate or publish to the Chamber the document and the Chamber can advise me of how it would like this handled, it's in exact condition from -- if I might ask the Chamber to consider at this time, until there is some system by which the originals will be handed to the Registry because I think it's a bit raw right now, the whole new rule. Also I have handed to Your Honours a declaration by the investigator as to the date and location of seizure on that particular document. That in its original form I'm very happy to leave with the Chamber, with copies to the Defence. The original document, if I may request to have it back at this time so that I can -- we can discuss with the Registry how we will implement the terms of this new rule. I think it's going to be a bit messy at first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do not have any fears, Ms. Somers. We will get -- we will look at the document, but with the view, of course --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- with the new rule and how to set it in motion. It has to be shown to Defence counsel as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There are a couple more, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There are a couple more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I didn't mean to cut you off. I want to make sure we get this done. The next document was 3/206 which was the rules on internal organisation of the Republic and Secretariat of the Interior dated January 1990, and this concerned the description of patrol sector leader's job. The next document, which was 3/207, for the same reasons, that it's a third person's statement, effectively a letter, we would withdraw any attempt to seek its admission. Questions -- this concerned the IPTF letter which had a term which was deemed to be inappropriate within its confines. We asked questions about it; I think that was sufficient. The next is 3/208, a list of workers providing security to Omarska Collection Centre, dated 21 June 1992. The last is 3/209; it is the reserve police station receipt of solemn oaths taken. I hope I have skipped nothing, but I believe that is the entire list of documents which we have put to the witness and would ask to have the Chamber admit them into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't seen the documents 3/187 and 3/205. What's happened with those?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Sorry, Your Honour. Those documents were not used, and we will not be asking the Court to consider them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. I think that now we can hear Mr. Simic. These documents were used during the Defence case of Mr. Kvocka. Documents 3/201 and 3/202 have already been admitted. We have to bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before I respond to the documents that have been tendered by my learned colleague, I have to say that we also discussed a document earlier on, number 3/176. This document was used during the cross-examination of Mr. Kvocka, and my colleague is now telling me that this document was not admitted. But I still don't know anything as to the fate of this document. Once again, let me say it's document 3/176. As regards the documents that have been tendered, I will first speak of those to which I object; that is, I will first give you the list of documents in respect of which I raise my objections. The first document being 3/201, that is the interview which was published in Slobodna Bosna in respect of which we already stated that it was never actually given and that Mr. Kvocka was never talking to Mr. Bennett as part of an interview. What was contained in the interview was, indeed, conveyed from that conversation. But Mr. Kvocka cannot say anything in respect to that, cannot state his position in respect to that, and the article was published two days after his arrest. Likewise, we object to document 3/202, that is, a radio programme which was broadcast by a radio station, Slobodne Prijedor. Mr. Kvocka never gave such an interview to this radio station. It is simply a compilation of various materials and documents which we already mentioned in relation to the interview with Mr. Chris Bennett. The third document to which we object is the document marked as 3/203, that is, the interview which Mr. Kvocka gave to the OTP, that is, to the investigators of the Tribunal. In objecting to this document, we have in mind the decision that the statements of witnesses will not be tendered into evidence as exhibits but that they can be used as the basis for the examination of witnesses. Mr. Kvocka is a Defence witness. My learned colleague had this document in her possession and she went through this document while cross-examining Mr. Kvocka. We believe that the same logic should be applied in respect of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Simic, but Madam Registrar has just told me that we have been working for an hour and a half. We can either have a ten-minute break and come back - but you know very well that we can never have only a ten-minute break in this case - so the other thing we can do is to finish as soon as possible or -- I really don't know what to do. What do the interpreters think? How do they feel? Yes, I know, but the Judges are also tired. I am tired as well. Let us try to finish within ten minutes. Is this acceptable to the interpreters? Yes, thank you very much. Let us try and do our best to finish as soon as possible. Even if we don't make a decision today, at least we have the facts necessary for us to make our ruling later on. Have you finished with 203?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence does not object to any other document being admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we are now only going to listen to your arguments for the purposes of collecting the necessary information for us to make the ruling, Ms. Somers. So what we have in dispute are documents 3/201, 3/202, and 3/203. How do you respond, Ms. Somers, to the objection raised by Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour, we already indicated that the Chamber has already admitted 3/201 and 3/202 so I think that those issues are moot as to those documents. Those were done pursuant to Mr. Kvocka's testimony. That's not before us. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The issue of Mr. Kvocka's previous voluntary statement in the presence of counsel, I think, should cause the Chamber no difficulties. From reading the language of decisions, what is contemplated, it appears, is it was a challenge to the -- it was a discussion on the orality of evidence. In this instance, an admission -- the admission of the accused's interview is, in no way, of -- in no way offends that principle because the accused testified. In fact, these questions from his voluntary statement in the presence of counsel, his voluntary interview in the presence of counsel, are perfectly consistent with the underlying concern about orality and, in fact, properly belong among the documents to be considered by this Chamber when the Chamber retires to deliberate. National systems would certainly permit this, and the idea of excluding third party hearsay statements, which I believe was one of the concerns of the ruling, is not an issue here. This is a statement that clearly was given by the accused, with all the safeguards that are required under any system which seeks to safeguard the rights of the accused, and the evidence has been put to him with these concerns in mind. I think that there is no doubt that this is a perfectly admissible statement and does not lie within any of the prohibitions that may have been issued by this Chamber concerning hearsay evidence, third party statements. That was not intended for this kind of document. Just to remind the Chamber, I believe that the statement of Mr. Prcac was also taken into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Ms. Somers. Madam Registrar, just to confirm, Exhibits 3/201 and 3/202, have they already been tendered before?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they were admitted by the Chamber on the 13th of February, 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Simic, your objection is now moot. You contested these --

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will withdraw my objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. As regards all of the exhibits, the Chamber can decide already that those exhibits which are not in dispute are admitted. Exhibit 3/203, which is in dispute, which has been objected to by the Defence, is going to be analysed by the Chamber and the Chamber will make an oral ruling during the following days. We have five minutes left and I would like to use it for something that I think has to be dealt with today. It regards the accused Kos. An application, a motion, was submitted on the 26th of January, a motion for protective measures in respect of one witness. A closed session was requested and the Prosecutor objected to the request made by the Defence. Then following that or at the same time, I don't know, a videolink was requested in respect of that witness. I should like to hear you, Mr. O'Sullivan, and I would like to know whether you have requested the videolink because the Prosecutor opposed protective measures, or if there is another reason for your request.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No. The request for videolink is not connected to the protective measures. The witness was put on the list of videolink -- request for videolink testimony in our amended witness list and witness order in which we reduced our witnesses down to five here, and we request one further witness, this other individual, DB-1, via videolink from Banja Luka. Those are all the witnesses we're intending to call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much, Mr. O'Sullivan. I don't want to risk prolonging this session. I think we will have to find another opportunity to continue this Status Conference because we will be exceeding the time limit. I do understand that the interpreters are tired, we are all tired, but thank you very much for having accepted to work longer to finish. Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I wouldn't ask the Chamber to delay at all today, but because Mr. Simic was kind enough to mention an exhibit, 3/176, may I have the time to check and see what that was? Apparently, we did make reference to it both in Basrak and in Kvocka, and I think we can take a look at whether there was a translation available. I don't want to take the Court's time today. I'll inform the Chamber if the Chamber gives me an opportunity at the end of another session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're quite right, Ms. Somers. Thank you for paying attention to this detail. I had a note regarding that issue, but I was in a hurry, I wanted to finish as soon as possible. We all need that particular piece of information, both Mr. Simic and the Chamber. Thank you very much. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Mr. Nikolic said that he would finish very early tomorrow, so we might perhaps continue with our Status Conference tomorrow as soon as Mr. Nikolic finishes his case. That's just a suggestion, Your Honour, that I wanted to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, gladly. I didn't know that. You are better informed than I am. If your information is correct, and I hope that it is, we can, of course, continue with our Status Conference as soon as Mr. Nikolic finishes his case. Thank you very much. See you tomorrow.
